interviewQuestions.question: What is continuous integration, and what problem does it actually solve?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
CI is two things happening together: developers merge small changes into a shared branch **frequently** — daily or more — and every merge gets **built and tested automatically**, with no human deciding whether to bother.

The problem it solves is integration risk. Before CI was standard, teams worked in long-lived branches and integrated everything near a release, which meant conflicts and regressions surfaced when there was the least time to fix them — the classic "integration hell." CI shrinks that risk by shrinking the batch size: if you merge a small change every few hours and verify it immediately, there's never a large pile of unverified work to reconcile.

Concretely, a PR triggers a pipeline — install dependencies, build, run tests, report pass/fail back on the PR — and branch protection makes that check required before merge is even possible. The signal has to be fast, too: a 3-minute pipeline gets trusted and run constantly; a 40-minute one gets batched around, which quietly recreates the exact problem CI exists to prevent.

So the shorthand I'd give: CI isn't a tool, it's an agreement that main stays green, verified continuously in small increments rather than in one large, late gamble.

**Testing:** whether you understand CI as a process discipline (small batches + automatic verification) rather than just "we have a build server."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide what should be a required, merge-blocking check versus something that runs after merge?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd draw the line on two things: **how fast the check is** and **how likely it is to be a false positive**. Anything that's both fast (order of minutes) and reliable — unit tests, linting, type checks, a build — belongs in the required path, because it gives the author an answer before they've context-switched away.

Anything slow or flaky by nature — full end-to-end browser suites, cross-service integration tests against real infrastructure, load or performance tests — I'd move out of the blocking path. Not because it's less important, but because putting it there makes the required pipeline slow enough that people start batching PRs to avoid running it, which undoes the whole point of CI. Those suites still run: on a schedule, on merge (non-blocking), or nightly, and failures get triaged with urgency, just not by holding up every author's merge.

A concrete example: a service with a 90-second unit-test suite and a 25-minute Selenium suite. I'd block merge on the 90-second suite plus lint and build, and run the Selenium suite post-merge, alerting the team if it goes red rather than gating every PR on it.

The trade-off is real: you accept a short window where a merged commit hasn't been end-to-end verified yet. That's acceptable because the fast checks already caught the large majority of regressions, and the slow suite still catches the rest — just a few minutes later.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about the cost/benefit of pipeline placement instead of treating "more required checks" as strictly safer.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Pipeline design

interviewQuestions.question: Your CI pipeline takes 45 minutes, and you've noticed engineers stacking three or four PRs before running it once. How do you fix this?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd treat this as the pipeline losing the property that makes it CI at all — if people are batching to avoid running it, they've already reverted to pre-CI behavior, and the batch is where the next integration-hell incident hides.

First step is diagnosis, not a rewrite: profile the pipeline to see where the 45 minutes actually goes. In my experience it's usually one of a few things — an unnecessarily serial pipeline that could fan out into parallel shards, a full end-to-end suite sitting in the blocking path, or a cold dependency install with no caching.

The fix is usually a combination: parallelize the test suite across shards so wall-clock time drops even if total test-CPU-time doesn't, cache dependencies and build layers between runs, and — most importantly — **move anything that isn't a fast, reliable check out of the required path** and run it asynchronously after merge. Target getting the required checks under 10 minutes; that's roughly the threshold where people stop feeling the urge to batch.

Just as important is the follow-through: once the pipeline is fast, I'd explicitly tell the team the batching workaround is no longer needed, and watch pipeline duration as an ongoing metric — it creeps back up quietly as more tests get added, and needs an owner the same way the codebase does.

**Testing:** whether you can connect a technical fix (parallelize, cache, retier) to the actual behavioral problem it's meant to solve.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Debugging

interviewQuestions.question: How would you set up branch protection for a shared repo used by 50 engineers?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from the invariant I actually want: **main is always green and always deployable**, and work backward to the rules that guarantee it.

Concretely: require the CI build/test check to pass, require at least one code-review approval, and require the branch to be up to date with main before merging — that last one matters more at 50 engineers than at 5, because the chance your branch was tested against a main that's now an hour stale is much higher. I'd also disable direct pushes to main entirely, so every change goes through a PR and its checks, no exceptions for "just a quick fix."

At this scale I'd add a couple of things a smaller team can skip: a CODEOWNERS-style rule so changes to sensitive paths (auth, payments, infra config) get a review from someone with context, and a merge queue or serialized-merge mechanism, because with 50 engineers merging concurrently, several PRs can each individually pass CI against main but conflict or break when combined — a merge queue re-verifies against the latest main right before landing, not just at PR-open time.

The trade-off is friction: more required gates slow down the last mile of every merge. I'd justify that against the alternative, which is main breaking often enough that the whole team's velocity drops far more than the few extra minutes per PR cost.

**Testing:** whether you can scale branch-protection thinking beyond a small team to the failure modes that only show up under real concurrency.
